title: Help yourself: --help, man and error messages
summary: Every tool explains itself. Read its help and its errors, and you never stay stuck for long.

scheme: [ ] = optional     ... = as many as you like
text: Almost every command answers --help with a short guide. The Usage line shows how to write it.
- Words in [ ] are optional: sort alone works, it reads what you type until Ctrl+D.
- ... means you can give several: sort a.txt b.txt sorts both together.

scheme: short long form           what it does
text: Below the Usage line, one line per option: a short form, a long form, and what it does. Both forms do the same thing.
- The list is long? Search it: grep -i finds a word whatever its case.
- "compare human readable numbers" means sizes written with a unit: 2K is smaller than 1G, even though 2 is bigger than 1.
- Or page through it: sort --help | less, q quits.
man opens the manual: longer than --help, with explanations, and some pages end with an EXAMPLES section.
- It opens in a pager: arrows scroll, /word searches, n jumps to the next match, q quits.
- man -k searches the one-line descriptions of all manuals, when you don't know the tool's name yet.

scheme: cat: notes.tx: No such file or directory
who  on what   what went wrong
text: An error message is a clue, not a punishment. Read it from left to right: which program, on what, what went wrong.
- command not found: a typo, or the tool isn't installed.
- No such file or directory: check the name and where you are (ls, pwd).
- Permission denied: the file exists, but you may not do that to it.
